When porting custom code from an old fork into a remade repo where the layout was completely restructured (e.g. src/snippets/inputs.ts, custom tools, agent loops, providers), matching by directory path fails.
Instead of matching paths, you need to match by functional exports / symbols.
Step 1: Generate an Autonomous Symbol & Migration Map
Run this script to scan the deprecated tau folder, extract all exported functions/classes/types, and automatically check where those concepts or symbols exist in the new fork:
bun -e '
import fs from "fs";
import path from "path";

// Usage: bun map-tau.ts <deprecated_tau_dir> <new_fork_dir>
const oldDir = process.argv[2] || "./deprecated";
const newDir = process.argv[3] || ".";

const IGNORE = new Set(["node_modules", ".git", "target", "dist", "build", ".next", ".turbo", "__pycache__"]);
const EXTENSIONS = new Set([".ts", ".js", ".py", ".rs"]);

function getFiles(dir) {
  const results = [];
  try {
    for (const entry of fs.readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true })) {
      if (IGNORE.has(entry.name) || entry.name.startsWith(".")) continue;
      const full = path.join(dir, entry.name);
      if (entry.isDirectory()) results.push(...getFiles(full));
      else if (entry.isFile() && EXTENSIONS.has(path.extname(entry.name))) results.push(full);
    }
  } catch {}
  return results;
}

console.log("Scanning old Tau fork...");
const oldFiles = getFiles(oldDir);
console.log("Scanning new remade fork...");
const newFiles = getFiles(newDir);

// Index all symbol declarations in the new fork
const newSymbolIndex = new Map(); // symbol -> newFilePath
for (const file of newFiles) {
  try {
    const text = fs.readFileSync(file, "utf-8");
    // Match export functions, classes, interfaces, types, def, fn
    const matches = text.matchAll(/(?:export\s+(?:default\s+)?(?:class|function|type|interface|const)|def\s+|fn\s+)\s*([a-zA-Z0-9_]+)/g);
    for (const m of matches) {
      newSymbolIndex.set(m[1], path.relative(newDir, file));
    }
  } catch {}
}

// Analyze each old file
const migrationReport = [];

for (const file of oldFiles) {
  try {
    const text = fs.readFileSync(file, "utf-8");
    const relOld = path.relative(oldDir, file);

    const exportedSymbols = [];
    const matches = text.matchAll(/(?:export\s+(?:default\s+)?(?:class|function|type|interface|const)|def\s+|fn\s+)\s*([a-zA-Z0-9_]+)/g);
    for (const m of matches) exportedSymbols.push(m[1]);

    // Find destination candidates based on overlapping symbols or basename
    const candidateDestinations = new Set();
    for (const sym of exportedSymbols) {
      if (newSymbolIndex.has(sym)) {
        candidateDestinations.add(newSymbolIndex.get(sym));
      }
    }

    const baseName = path.basename(file);
    const sameNameMatches = newFiles
      .filter(nf => path.basename(nf) === baseName)
      .map(nf => path.relative(newDir, nf));

    sameNameMatches.forEach(m => candidateDestinations.add(m));

    migrationReport.push({
      oldFile: relOld,
      symbols: exportedSymbols,
      targets: Array.from(candidateDestinations),
      isOrphan: candidateDestinations.size === 0 && exportedSymbols.length > 0
    });
  } catch {}
}

// Display results
console.log("\n=======================================================");
console.log("TAU FORK MIGRATION MAP (BY EXPORTED SYMBOLS)");
console.log("=======================================================\n");

const mapped = migrationReport.filter(r => r.targets.length > 0);
const orphans = migrationReport.filter(r => r.isOrphan);

console.log(`[+] Directly Mapped (${mapped.length} files):`);
for (const item of mapped) {
  console.log(`  OLD: ${item.oldFile}`);
  console.log(`  NEW: ${item.targets.join(", ")}`);
  console.log(`  SYM: [${item.symbols.slice(0, 5).join(", ")}${item.symbols.length > 5 ? "..." : ""}]\n`);
}

console.log(`\n[!] Custom / Orphaned Features to Port (${orphans.length} files):`);
for (const item of orphans) {
  console.log(`  * ${item.oldFile} (Exports: ${item.symbols.join(", ")})`);
}

fs.writeFileSync("tau_migration_map.json", JSON.stringify(migrationReport, null, 2));
console.log("\nFull mapping written to ./tau_migration_map.json");
' "$DEP" "."

Step 2: How to Handle the Output
 * Directly Mapped Files (targets.length > 0):
   These are existing modules that were reorganized or renamed (e.g. your old inputs.ts might map to src/tui/input.ts or src/cli/prompt.ts in the remake). You can run a 3-way diff or view the git differences:
   # Compare the old custom implementation against the new fork's version:
diff -u "$DEP/src/snippets/inputs.ts" "./src/path/to/new_input.ts" | less

 * Orphaned Custom Features (isOrphan: true):
   These are the custom features you built (new tools, custom agent pipelines, specialized parsers) that have no counterpart in the remade fork.
   * Pick a dedicated home for custom additions in the new structure (e.g. src/extensions/, src/plugins/, or src/custom/).
   * Copy just the orphan files over cleanly without overwriting the core architecture of the new fork.
Step 3: Fast Diff if Both Are Git Commits
If your deprecated version was previously committed to git before the remake:
# Compare the branch/commit prior to the remake against current HEAD
# only listing modified/added files, ignoring unchanged upstream code:
git diff --name-status <commit-before-remake>..HEAD

Or extract the exact list of files added exclusively in your previous fork:
git log <upstream/main>..<old-fork-branch> --name-only --oneline | grep -v '^[a-f0-9]' | sort -u

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""buildsrvd — the fleet's continuous-modification engine.

A pitchfork-managed build daemon (stdlib-only Python). It watches a
disk-backed job queue, runs builds through the user's login shell
(`bash -lc`, so mise toolchains resolve exactly as they do for Chris),
streams logs to per-job files, and caches artifacts keyed by content hash
of the job spec.

Job semantics (forward-only):
  * The daemon NEVER touches the working tree — no git checkout, stash,
    or revert. The build command sees the tree exactly as it is.
  * Jobs iterate forward on the tree; re-submitting an identical job is
    a cache-hit no-op that returns the previous result.
  * Interrupted jobs (daemon restart mid-run) are re-queued cleanly;
    nothing is ever half-applied because nothing is applied at all —
    only the build command runs.

Layout under $BUILDSRV_ROOT (default /home/toxic/buildsrv):
  queue/      pending job specs: <id>.json
  active/     claimed by this daemon (moved back to queue/ on boot)
  logs/       <id>.log — streamed while the build runs, tail-able
  results/    <id>.json — terminal result record
  artifacts/  <jobhash>/ — copied build outputs + manifest.json
  state.json  job ledger (status, attempts, hashes, timings)

Health: http://127.0.0.1:$BUILDSRV_PORT/health
"""
import hashlib
import json
import os
import shutil
import signal
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from pathlib import Path

# Crash forensics (2026-09-17): the daemon died 3x with no traceback and
# no OOM mark. Make the next death observable: faulthandler dumps C-level
# crashes to stderr, excepthooks log uncaught Python exceptions from any
# thread, and SIGHUP is logged instead of silently killing (default HUP
# action terminates with no trace).
import faulthandler
import traceback as _tb

faulthandler.enable()

arguments.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

REPO_DIR="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null || pwd)"
REPO_NAME="$(basename "$REPO_DIR")"
BUILDSRV_ROOT="${BUILDSRV_ROOT:-/home/toxic/buildsrv}"
QUEUE_DIR="$BUILDSRV_ROOT/queue"

mkdir -p "$QUEUE_DIR"

COMMIT_SHA="$(git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo "manual")"
JOB_ID="push-${REPO_NAME}-${COMMIT_SHA:0:7}-${RANDOM}"

# Detect toolchain
TOOLCHAIN="bun"
if [ -f "$REPO_DIR/Cargo.toml" ]; then
    TOOLCHAIN="rust"
elif [ -f "$REPO_DIR/go.mod" ]; then
    TOOLCHAIN="go"
elif [ -f "$REPO_DIR/pyproject.toml" ] || [ -f "$REPO_DIR/requirements.txt" ]; then
    TOOLCHAIN="python"
fi

# Detect build command
BUILD_CMD="bun run build"
if [ "$TOOLCHAIN" = "rust" ]; then
    BUILD_CMD="cargo build --release"
elif [ "$TOOLCHAIN" = "go" ]; then
    BUILD_CMD="go build -v ./..."
elif [ "$TOOLCHAIN" = "python" ]; then
    BUILD_CMD="python3 -m build || pip install ."
fi

cat <<EOF > "$QUEUE_DIR/${JOB_ID}.json"
{
  "id": "$JOB_ID",
  "name": "push-${REPO_NAME}-${COMMIT_SHA:0:7}",
  "repo": "$REPO_DIR",
  "toolchain": "$TOOLCHAIN",
  "cmd": "$BUILD_CMD"
}
EOF

echo "🚀 [CI/CD Push Build] Submitted job ${JOB_ID} for ${REPO_NAME} (${COMMIT_SHA:0:7}) to buildsrv queue."

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

REPO_DIR="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null || pwd)"
REPO_NAME="$(basename "$REPO_DIR")"
BUILDSRV_ROOT="${BUILDSRV_ROOT:-/home/toxic/buildsrv}"
QUEUE_DIR="$BUILDSRV_ROOT/queue"

mkdir -p "$QUEUE_DIR"

COMMIT_SHA="$(git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo "manual")"

# Extract version if package.json exists
VERSION="unknown"
if [ -f "$REPO_DIR/package.json" ]; then
    VERSION="$(node -p "require('./package.json').version || 'unknown'" 2>/dev/null || echo "unknown")"
elif [ -f "$REPO_DIR/packages/coding-agent/package.json" ]; then
    VERSION="$(node -p "require('./packages/coding-agent/package.json').version || 'unknown'" 2>/dev/null || echo "unknown")"
fi

JOB_ID="v${VERSION}-${REPO_NAME}-${COMMIT_SHA:0:7}-${RANDOM}"

# Detect toolchain
TOOLCHAIN="bun"
if [ -f "$REPO_DIR/Cargo.toml" ]; then
    TOOLCHAIN="rust"
elif [ -f "$REPO_DIR/go.mod" ]; then
    TOOLCHAIN="go"
elif [ -f "$REPO_DIR/pyproject.toml" ] || [ -f "$REPO_DIR/requirements.txt" ]; then
    TOOLCHAIN="python"
fi

# Detect build command
BUILD_CMD="bun run build"
if [ "$TOOLCHAIN" = "rust" ]; then
    BUILD_CMD="cargo build --release"
elif [ "$TOOLCHAIN" = "go" ]; then
    BUILD_CMD="go build -v ./..."
elif [ "$TOOLCHAIN" = "python" ]; then
    BUILD_CMD="python3 -m build || pip install ."
fi

cat <<EOF > "$QUEUE_DIR/${JOB_ID}.json"
{
  "id": "$JOB_ID",
  "name": "v${VERSION}-${REPO_NAME}-${COMMIT_SHA:0:7}",
  "repo": "$REPO_DIR",
  "toolchain": "$TOOLCHAIN",
  "cmd": "$BUILD_CMD"
}
EOF

echo "🚀 [CI/CD Push Build] Submitted versioned build job ${JOB_ID} (v${VERSION}) for ${REPO_NAME} (${COMMIT_SHA:0:7}) to buildsrv queue."

Pin the active set with `--tools read,edit,bash,…`; rarely used discoverable tools stay behind `xd://` devices. `read xd://` lists them, and `write xd://` runs one when `tools.xdev` is enabled. 271: 272:**Files & search** 273: 274:- `read` — files, dirs, archives, SQLite, PDFs, notebooks, URLs, remote `ssh://` paths, and internal `://` schemes through one path. 275:- `write` — create or overwrite a file, archive entry, or SQLite row. 276:- `edit` — hashline patches with content-hash anchors and stale-anchor recovery. 277:- `ast_edit` — structural rewrites previewed before apply, via ast-grep. 278:- `ast_grep` — structural code queries over 50+ tree-sitter grammars. 279:- `grep` — regex over files, globs, and internal URLs. 280:- `glob` — glob-based path lookup; reach for `grep` when you need content matches. 281: 282:**Runtime** 283: 284:- `bash` — workspace shell with 46 in-process coreutils, optional PTY, and background-job dispatch. 285:- `eval` — persistent Python and JavaScript cells with shared prelude and tool re-entry. 286: 287:**Code intelligence** 288: 289:- `lsp` — diagnostics, navigation, symbols, renames, code actions, raw requests. 290:- `debug` — drive a DAP session — breakpoints, stepping, threads, stack, variables. 291:- `security_scan` — plan and run native security reviews; optionally promote it into a managed skill. 318:- `manage_skill` — create, update, or delete an isolated managed skill. 319: 320:Setting-gated, off by default: `github`, `security_scan`, `generate_image`, `tts`, `checkpoint`, `rewind`, and the memory tools (`retain`/`recall`/`reflect`/`memory_edit`, per `memory.backend`). 321: 322:[Full reference →](https://omp.sh/docs/tools) 323: 324:### Prompt controls 325: 326:Three standalone, lowercase words opt a turn into specialized agent behavior: 327: 328:- `ultrathink` — request careful multi-step reasoning and the highest supported automatic thinking effort. 329:- `orchestrate` — run substantial independent work through parallel subagents and verify each phase. 330:- `workflowz` — build a deterministic multi-subagent workflow with the active `task` tool. 331: 332:They trigger only in prose, not inside code spans, fenced code blocks, XML/HTML sections, identifiers, or paths. A coding agent with the IDE wired in. omp.sh

Built by Stencil Labs · Fork of Pi by @mariozechner

## Sovereign / Ranch Fork Enhancements This sovereign fork incorporates advanced local extensions and mesh integrations over upstream `oh-my-pi` (`v18.3.0`): - **VansRouter Integration**: Native source-owned runtime integration with canonical `.secrets` loading and optimized multi-provider model routing. - **Kimi Code Daemon Integration**: Bundled `@moonshot-ai/kimi-code` source integration with build scripts and robust daemon lifecycle supervision via Pitchfork. - **Immutable Binary Pinning**: Hardened launcher pinning (`omp-pin`) preventing unintentional auto-update clobbering and protecting the fork engine runtime. - **Mesh & Port SSOT Alignment**: Strict adherence to the 25xxx port registry and zero hardcoded port allocations. The most capable agent surface that ships. Continuously tuned by real-world use — complete out of the box, open all the way down. **60+** providers · **31** built-in tools · **14** lsp ops · **28** dap ops · **~80k** lines of Rust core. > [!NOTE] > Pull requests are **temporarily open to everyone** as a trial. We previously > required a vouch before accepting PRs; that requirement is lifted for now > while we evaluate how open contributions go. Depending on the results, the > vouch system may return. ## Install **macOS · Linux** ```sh curl -fsSL https://omp.sh/install | sh ``` > **Alpine / musl:** the prebuilt musl binary links `libstdc++`/`libgcc` dynamically, which stock Alpine does not ship. Install them first: `apk add libstdc++ libgcc`. **Homebrew** ```sh brew install can1357/tap/omp ``` **Bun (recommended)** ```sh bun install -g @oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent ``` **Nix** ```sh # Run without installing nix run github:can1357/oh-my-pi # Or install into the active profile nix profile install github:can1357/oh-my-pi ``` Flake consumers can use `packages..omp`, `overlays.default`, `nixosModules.default`, or `homeManagerModules.default`. A Home Manager configuration can install OMP and own its settings declaratively: ```nix { inputs.omp.url = "github:can1357/oh-my-pi"; # In your Home Manager module: imports = [ inputs.omp.homeManagerModules.default ]; programs.omp = { enable = true; settings.startup.quiet = true; }; } ``` **Windows (PowerShell)** ```powershell irm https://omp.sh/install.ps1 | iex ``` **Pinned versions (mise)** ```sh mise use -g github:can1357/oh-my-pi ``` macOS · Linux · Windows · bun ≥ 1.3.14 ### Shell completions `omp` generates its own completion scripts for **bash**, **zsh**, and **fish** from the live command/flag metadata, so they never drift from the actual CLI. Subcommands, flags, and enum values complete statically; model names (`--model`, `--smol`, `--slow`, `--plan`) resolve against the bundled model catalog and `--resume` against your on-disk sessions. ```sh # zsh — add to ~/.zshrc (or write the output into a file on your $fpath) eval "$(omp completions zsh)" # bash — add to ~/.bashrc eval "$(omp completions bash)" # fish omp completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/omp.fish ``` ## Every tool, _benchmaxxed_. Edits that land on the first attempt. Reads that summarize files instead of dumping their content. Searches that return instantly. Pick any model — omp will get it right. | model | metric | what | | ---------------- | ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Grok Code Fast 1 | 6.7% → 68.3% | Tenfold lift the moment the edit format stops eating the model alive. | | Gemini 3 Flash | +5 pp | Over str_replace — beats Google's own best attempt at the format. | | Grok 4 Fast | −61% tokens | Output collapses once the retry loop on bad diffs disappears. | | MiniMax | 2.1× | Pass rate more than doubles. Same weights, same prompt. | - `read` : summarized snippets · ideal defaults · selector hit rate - `grep` : fastest in the west - `lsp` : everything your IDE knows, the agent knows - `prompts` : adjusted relentlessly for each model [Read the full post ↗](https://blog.can.ac/2026/02/12/the-harness-problem/) ## The Pi _you love_, with **batteries included**. Originally built on [Mario Zechner](https://github.com/mariozechner)'s wonderful [Pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono), omp adds everything you're missing. ### 01 · Code execution w/ tool-calling Most harnesses give the agent a Python sandbox and call it done. Ours runs persistent Python and a Bun worker, and either kernel can call back into the agent's own tools — read, search, task — over a loopback bridge. The agent loads a CSV with tool.read from inside Python, charts it from JavaScript, and never leaves the cell. ![omp TUI running Python code and rendering a chart.](assets/python.webp) ### 02 · LSP wired into every write Ask for a rename and you get a rename. The call goes through workspace/willRenameFiles, so re-exports, barrel files, and aliased imports update before the file moves. Everything your IDE knows, the agent knows. ![omp TUI with TypeScript and Biome language servers active.](assets/lspv.webp) _[Read the LSP config docs](docs/lsp-config.md)_ ### 03 · Drives a real debugger A C binary segfaults: the agent attaches lldb, steps to the bad pointer, reads the frame. A Go service hangs: it attaches dlv and walks the goroutines. A Python process is wedged: debugpy, pause, inspect, evaluate. Most agents are still sprinkling print statements. ![omp TUI: a live lldb-dap session against a native binary at /tmp/omp-native/demo. Adapter=lldb-dap, Status=stopped, Frame=xorshift32, Instruction pointer 0x10000055C, Location demo.c:6:10. Debug scopes and Debug variables cards show locals (x = 57351) and the agent confirms the math: x went from 7 → 57351 (= 7 ^ (7<<13)).](https://omp.sh/clips/dap-poster.webp) _[Watch the capture ↗](https://omp.sh/clips/dap.mp4)_ ### 04 · Time-traveling stream rules Your rules sit dormant until the model goes off-script. A regex match aborts the stream mid-token, injects the rule as a system reminder, and retries from the same point. You get course-correction without paying context tax on every turn. content cleaning | html-to-markdown-rs | 60 | | sixel | Terminal image rendering · decode PNG · JPEG · WebP · GIF · resize · SIXEL encode | icy_sixel · image | 55 | ## Four entry points: _interactive_, _one-shot_, RPC, and ACP. Same engine, four wrappers. `omp` runs the TUI. `omp -p` answers a single prompt and exits. The Node SDK embeds the session in your process. `omp --mode rpc` and `omp acp` hand the wheel to another program over stdio. ### Interactive — when in doubt, the agent asks The TUI is the default surface. Tool calls render as cards, edits preview before they land, and ambiguity routes through the `ask` tool — a structured option picker the agent can call mid-turn. The keyboard handles the rest. The same prompt cards surface over ACP, so editors get the picker without writing one. ![omp TUI showing a multi-select question from the ask tool.](assets/ask.webp) ### SDK — embed in Node `@oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent` Node and TypeScript hosts pull the engine in directly. The package exposes `ModelRegistry`, `SessionManager`, `createAgentSession`, and `discoverAuthStorage`; the session emits typed events you subscribe to. ```ts import { ModelRegistry, SessionManager, createAgentSession, discoverAuthStorage, } from "@oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent"; const auth = await discoverAuthStorage(); const models = new ModelRegistry(auth); await models.refresh(); const { session } = await createAgentSession({ sessionManager: SessionManager.inMemory(), authStorage: auth, modelRegistry: models, }); await session.prompt("list .ts files"); ``` ### RPC — drive over stdio `omp --mode rpc` For non-Node embedders, or when you want process isolation. NDJSON commands in, response and event frames out. `--mode rpc-ui` adds tool cards, selectors, and dialogs as `extension_ui_request` frames the host must answer. ``` $ omp --mode rpc --no-session > {"id":"r1","type":"prompt","message":"list .ts files"} < {"id":"r1","type":"response", ...} > {"id":"r2","type":"set_model","provider":"anthropic","modelId":"sonnet-4.5"} > {"id":"r3","type":"abort"} ``` ### ACP — speak to editors `omp acp` The [Agent Client Protocol](https://github.com/zed-industries/agent-client-protocol) over JSON-RPC. When the editor advertises capabilities, tool I/O routes through it and writes are gated by `session/request_permission`. | omp tool | ACP route | | ------------ | ----------------------------------- | | `bash` | `terminal/create + terminal/output` | | `read` | `fs/read_text_file` | | `write` | `fs/write_text_file` | | `edit, bash` | `session/request_permission` | Full reference: [omp.sh/docs/sdk](https://omp.sh/docs/sdk). ## A harness worth keeping is one you _don't_ outgrow. Pick it up at **[omp.sh](https://omp.sh)**. omp is a fork of [Pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono) by [Mario Zechner](https://github.com/mariozechner), rewritten as a coding-first surface: sessions, subagents, slash commands, extensions — all TypeScript, all MIT, all on [GitHub](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi). Shape it from config, hook it from outside, or read the source when you need to. ### Primitives An extension is a TypeScript module. Same tool API, same slash-command registry, same hotkey table, same TUI primitives the built-ins use. Nothing is reserved. ### Discovery On first run omp inherits whatever is already on disk: rules, skills, and MCP servers from `.claude`, `.cursor`, `.windsurf`, `.gemini`, `.codex`, `.cline`, `.github/copilot`, and `.vscode`. No migration script. ### Extensibility Ask omp to write the piece you're missing, then `/reload-plugins`. Keep it local, ship it in a `marketplace`, or publish it to npm. ## Philosophy omp is a fork of [pi-mono](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono) by [Mario Zechner](https://github.com/mariozechner), extended with a batteries-included coding workflow. Key ideas: - Keep interactive terminal-first UX for real coding work - Include practical built-ins (tools, sessions, branching, subagents, extensibility) - Make advanced behavior configurable rather than hidden --- ## Development ### Getting started from source Fresh clones need both workspace dependencies and the local Rust/N-API addon before the source CLI can start. ```sh bun setup bun dev ``` `bun setup` installs Bun workspaces and builds `@oh-my-pi/pi-natives`. Re-run `bun run build:native` after changing Rust crates or `packages/natives`. Nix users get the pinned Bun and Rust toolchains plus all native build dependencies: ```sh nix develop bun setup bun dev ``` Build and smoke-test the distributable Nix package with `nix build .#omp`. Wayland screencast support is off by default (linking libpipewire adds ~750 MB of runtime closure); enable it with `omp.override { withWaylandScreencast = true; }`. `nix/bun.nix` is generated only when `bun.lock` changes; releases regenerate it automatically. For dependency changes, run: ```sh bun run gen:nix ``` The command uses `bun2nix` from `nix develop` when available, otherwise enters the development shell through Nix, then falls back to the pinned `bunx bun2nix@2.1.2`. Do not edit `nix/bun.nix` manually. For a non-interactive smoke check: ```sh bun dev -- --version ``` ### Debug Command `/debug` opens tools for debugging, reporting, and profiling. fi

export NIM_BASE_URL="${NIM_BASE_URL:-http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1}"

export RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH="$HOME/.ripgreprc"

export PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR=$HOME/.tau

# OMP & Tau Sovereign Environment Variables Reference

This reference documents every known environment variable supported by the Tau coding agent engine (`omp`), categorized by functional subsystem. 

---

## 1. Upstream Engine & Core Runtime Variables

| Variable | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `PI_CONFIG_DIR` | `$HOME/.omp` | Base configuration directory (overridden to `$HOME/.tau` in sovereign profiles). |
| `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` | `$PI_CONFIG_DIR/agent` | Storage directory for agent sessions, databases, and history. |
| `PI_PROFILE` | `default` | Active configuration profile name. |
| `PI_TIMING` | unset | Enables high-resolution performance and module load time tracing. |
| `PI_DEBUG_STARTUP` | unset | Enables verbose startup and initialization logs. |
| `PI_BUNDLED` | unset | Internal flag indicating whether the binary is running as a bundled distribution. |
| `PI_COMPILED` | unset | Indicates binary compilation mode. |
| `PI_PACKAGE_DIR` | unset | Root package directory override. |
| `PI_NO_TITLE` | unset | Suppresses dynamic TUI title updates. |
| `PI_NO_THINKING_LOOP_GUARD` | unset | Disables the internal loop guard for assistant thinking blocks. |
| `PI_TEST_NO_NATIVES` | unset | Forces fallback to pure JS/TS implementations instead of native N-API addons. |
| `PI_TOKENIZER_ACCURATE` | unset | Enables accurate BPE token counting mode. |
| `PI_TUI_RAW_BACKSPACE_IS_CTRL` | unset | Configures raw backspace interpretation in the TUI terminal interface. |

---

## 2. Streaming, Timeout, & Token Limits

| Variable | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `PI_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` | `5000` (pinned to `120000`) | Maximum idle time allowed while waiting for model stream events before watchdog aborts. |
| `PI_STREAM_FIRST_EVENT_TIMEOUT_MS` | `30000` (pinned to `300000`) | Timeout threshold for receiving the first response event during deep prompt prefill. |
| `PI_OPENAI_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` | `4096` (pinned to `32000`) | Raises maximum output token limits for OpenAI and OpenRouter gateways. |

---

## 3. Editing & Patching Behavior

| Variable | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `PI_STRICT_EDIT_MODE` | `false` (pinned to `true`) | Enforces strict hashline and anchor validation. |
| `PI_EDIT_FUZZY` | `true` | Enables fuzzy matching for patch anchor resolution. |
| `PI_EDIT_FUZZY_THRESHOLD` | `0.95` | Similarity threshold for fuzzy patch matching. |
| `PI_EDIT_VARIANT` | default | Selects alternative edit rendering or patch strategies. |

---

## 4. Provider Integrations & Gateways

| Variable | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `PI_AI_ANTIGRAVITY_VERSION` | `4.3.0` | Client version header sent to Antigravity backend. |
| `PI_AI_ANTIGRAVITY_ARCH` | `x64` | Target architecture reported to Antigravity. |
| `PI_AI_ANTIGRAVITY_OS` | `linux` | Operating system reported to Antigravity. |
| `PI_AI_CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION` | unset | Claude Code compatibility version string. |
| `PI_AI_GEMINI_CLI_VERSION` | unset | Gemini CLI compatibility version string. |
| `PI_PERPLEXITY_MODEL` | unset | Default model override for Perplexity search integration. |
| `PI_PERPLEXITY_API_MODEL` | unset | API model identifier for Perplexity backend. |
| `PI_PERPLEXITY_RESPONSES` | unset | Response formatting mode for Perplexity queries. |
| `PI_TINY_DEVICE` | `auto` | Device target for tiny transformers (`cpu` / `gpu`). |
| `PI_TINY_TRANSFORMERS_VERSION` | unset | Version string for local embedding transformers. |

---

## 5. Memory & Mnemopi / Hindsight Engines

| Variable | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `MNEMOPI_DATA_DIR` | `$HOME/.tau/blobs` | SQLite blob and vector storage directory. |
| `MNEMOPI_AUTO_MIGRATE` | `true` | Automatically runs database migrations on startup. |
| `MNEMOPI_LLM_ENABLED` | `true` | Enables local LLM assistance for memory summarization. |
| `MNEMOPI_LLM_BASE_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:25117` | Local LLM / Hindsight endpoint URL. |
| `MNEMOPI_EMBEDDING_MODEL` | unset | Model identifier for local vector embeddings. |
| `MNEMOPI_EXTRACTION_MODEL` | unset | Model identifier for memory fact extraction. |
| `MNEMOPI_FTS_WEIGHT` | unset | Full-text search ranking weight in SQLite. |
| `MNEMOPI_VEC_WEIGHT` | unset | Vector similarity ranking weight. |

# Sovereign / Ranch Fork Environment Variables Reference

This reference documents custom, source-owned environment variables introduced specifically in the **Sovereign / Ranch** fork (`sovereign/projects/tau`, `buildsrv`, `herd`, `shep`, and mesh infrastructure).

---

## 1. Mesh, Port SSOT, & Infrastructure Daemons

| Variable | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `HINDRA_API_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:25117` | Endpoint URL for the local Hindsight knowledge mesh daemon. |
| `BUILDSRV_PORT` | `25148` | Port for the Pitchfork-managed `buildsrv` compilation daemon. |
| `PAPER_POLLER_PORT` | `25149` | Port for the HFT-style arXiv/alphaXiv paper poller daemon. |
| `ANTIGRAVITY_USER_AGENT_VERSION` | `4.3.0` | Sovereign override for Antigravity backend protocol headers. |

---

## 2. CI/CD Push-Building & Automation

| Variable | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `BUILDSRV_ROOT` | `/home/toxic/buildsrv` | Root directory for `buildsrv` job queues, active runs, logs, and compiled binary caches. |
| `OMP_NATIVE_CARGO_PROFILE` | `local` | Cargo profile override (`local` / `release`) optimized for Zen 4 native target architectures. |
| `RUSTFLAGS` | `-C target-cpu=native -C link-arg=-fuse-ld=mold` | Compiler performance flags enforcing mold linker and native CPU optimizations. |

---

## 3. Custom Integration & Wrapper Flags

# Upstream Autonomy & Fork Synchronization Architecture

To maintain a clean fork basis while retaining sovereign autonomy and seamless upstream syncing against `can1357/oh-my-pi`, we employ a decoupled **Vendor-Overlay / Overlay-Patch** workflow.

---

## 1. Preserving Upstream Autonomy (`vendor` Remote)

1. **Explicit Upstream Tracking**:
   The upstream repository is tracked as a dedicated git remote:
   ```sh
   git remote add vendor https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi.git
   ```

2. **Clean Fast-Forward Merges (`vendor/main`)**:
   When upstream releases new versions, pull directly without local commit pollution:
   ```sh
   git fetch vendor
   git merge vendor/main --no-edit
   ```

---

## 2. Isolating Custom Fork Features

To prevent merge conflicts during upstream pulls, sovereign-specific enhancements are organized into:
- **Dedicated Plugins / Extensions** (`projects/ranch/herd`, `flock`, `shep`, `router`).
- **Custom Helper Scripts** (`sovereign/helpers/`).
- **Config Overrides** (`~/.tau/config.yml`, `~/.tau/sovereign-env.sh`).
- **Isolated Documentation** (`projects/tau/docs/upstream/` vs custom fork docs).

---

## 3. Automated CI/CD Upstream Sync & Push Building

Our automated CI/CD pipeline (`buildsrv` on port `25148` + Git `post-commit` hooks) ensures that:
- Every commit or upstream merge triggers an automated background build.
- Version tracking (`v18.3.0`) and content hashes cache artifacts cleanly.
- Immutable binary pinning (`omp-pin`) prevents upstream updates from breaking local paths.

That is a profoundly clarifying question. The reason we keep bumping into this confusion is because **we are mixing two totally different monorepo paradigms**:

1. **The Upstream Monorepo (`can1357/oh-my-pi` aka `tau`):** 
   - This is a *Bun/Rust workspace* monorepo where packages live under `packages/*` and Rust crates under `crates/*`.
   - Its root `package.json` uses `"workspaces": ["packages/*", ...]` to manage everything in one tree.

2. **The Sovereign Mesh Monorepo (`/home/toxic/estate`):**
   - This is an *infrastructure-level* multi-repo workspace where independent services (`herd`, `shep`, `ranch`, `tau`) live as subprojects or submodules under `projects/` and `tools/`.

### What do people actually use for monorepos?
- **Bun Workspaces / pnpm Workspaces:** For TypeScript/JavaScript monorepos, where a single root `package.json` with `"workspaces"` handles linking packages automatically.
- **Cargo Workspaces (`Cargo.toml` with `members`):** For Rust monorepos, allowing multiple crates to share dependencies and build targets.
- **Git Submodules or Subtrees:** For ecosystem meshes (like Ranch/Sovereign) where separate repositories need to be pinned together without losing their upstream commit history.

### Why our workflow drifted:
When we jump between `/home/toxic/estate` (the mesh root) and `/home/toxic/estate/projects/tau` (the actual Tau monorepo root), we confuse *infrastructure orchestration* (Pitchfork/mise) with *package compilation* (Bun/Cargo workspaces).

### The Fix:
- Treat `/home/toxic/estate/projects/tau` as the **self-contained package root** for Tau.
- Run all Bun workspace installs, builds, and tests directly inside `/home/toxic/estate/projects/tau`.
- Let the sovereign root (`/home/toxic/estate`) act solely as the **mesh orchestrator** via `mise.toml` and `pitchfork.toml`.

That clear separation keeps our tools aligned with standard monorepo practices and stops the path confusion once and for all.

In **September 2026**, the state-of-the-art monorepo stack has completely shifted away from traditional npm/yarn/pnpm workspaces or slow multi-tool setups. Here is what modern engineering teams actually use right now:

### 1. The Package Manager & Runtime: **Bun (v1.4+)**
- **Why:** Bun has won the JavaScript/TypeScript monorepo race for speed. Workspace resolution is lightning-fast, native SQLite is built-in, and it handles cross-package dependency linking instantly without hoisting headaches.
- **Config:** A root `package.json` with standard workspace globs:
  ```json
  "workspaces": ["packages/*", "crates/*"]
  ```

### 2. The Build Orchestrator: **Turborepo or Nx (with Rust-native caching)**
- **Why:** In 2026, no one waits for redundant builds. Turborepo / Nx track dependency graphs across TS and Rust crates, caching build outputs locally and remotely. 
- **The Setup:** Combined with our `buildsrv` daemon and NVMe-backed `sccache`/`uv` caches, workspace builds execute sub-second incremental builds.

### 3. Polyglot Stitching: **Cargo Workspaces + Bun Workspaces**
- For hybrid Rust + TypeScript monorepos (like Tau/OMP):
  - **Rust crates** are declared in the root `Cargo.toml` under `members = ["crates/*"]`.
  - **TS packages** are declared in root `package.json` under `"workspaces"`.
  - **N-API / Native Bridges** bind the Rust core (`pi-natives`) straight into Bun via napi-rs, compiling native addons on the fly (`bun run build:native`).

### 4. Git Layer: **Jujutsu (`jj`) or Modern Git Worktrees**
- Moving away from clunky git submodules, 2026 monorepos heavily leverage **Jujutsu (`jj`)** or isolated workspace worktrees (`/tmp` or `~/.local/share/worktrees`) so multiple agents or developers can mutate subtrees concurrently without locking the working copy.

**Build Systems & Monorepo Tools 2026 — Bazel 8 · Pants 2 · Buck2 · Nx 20 · Turborepo 2 · Moon · Lerna 8 · Rush · pnpm Workspaces Deep Dive | Chaos and Order**: Here’s a concise briefing focused on 2026 monorepo tooling trends, especially Bun, Turborepo, and Nx, as covered in the article:

- 2026 landscape: Monorepo tools split into two main camps
  - Polyglot/build-system camp: Bazel 8, Buck2, Pants 2 — strong for multi-language, large-scale repos with declarative graphs and cross-language dependencies.
  - JS/TS-centric camp: Turborepo 2 and Nx 20 (with Moon as a rising polyglot option) — optimized for JavaScript/TypeScript, ease of use, and integration with modern JS tooling.

- Nx 20 (Nrwl)
  - Focus: JS/TS-heavy monorepos with expanding polyglot support via plugins.
  - New/features: Atomizer (test splitting), Custom Conformance Rules, Self-Healing CI; post-Lerna integration solidifies Nx as the “monorepo platform” for many teams.
  - Position: Rich tooling, governance, and policy enforcement for mid-to-large JS/TS stacks; integrates with Nx Cloud for distributed caching and governance.

- Turborepo 2
  - Focus: Simple, fast task running with cache; strong DX and Next.js/Remix-oriented teams.
  - New/features: Rewritten core in Rust (2.x); strong remote caching through Vercel integration; easy setup with turbo.json and TURBO_TOKEN/TURBO_TEAM for CI/remote cache.
  - Position: Lowest-friction option for JS/TS teams wanting speed and Vercel-friendly workflows; attractive for Next.js ecosystems.

- Moon
  - Focus: Polyglot monorepo tool aiming to unify JS/TS, Python, Rust, Go, Deno, Bun under one tool.
  - Position: Language-agnostic orchestration with TOML-based toolchain pinning; competes in the polyglot, large-scale space alongside Bazel/Buck2/Pants.

- Practical takeaways by team profile
  - Small JS teams (~5 people): pnpm workspaces (simple) or Turborepo 2 for faster CI/remote caching in Next.js-heavy stacks.
  - Mid-size JS/TS teams with strong cloud/Next.js focus: Turborepo 2 + Vercel Remote Cache or Nx 20 for richer policy/tooling.
  - Mid-to-large teams needing governance and polyglot support: Nx 20 or Moon for broader language support and advanced conformance rules.
  - Large polyglot or poly-language requirements: Bazel 8 / Buck2 / Pants 2 for declarative graphs and cross-language build policies.
  - JVM-heavy teams: Gradle 8.10 with Develocity or Maven 4 with mvnd; consider how they pair with the JS monorepo tools if needed.

- Quick guidance by scenario (from the article’s quick guide)
  - Small JS team: pnpm workspaces alone.
  - Mid-size JS/TS + Next

**The 2026 Monorepo: Bun 1.3, Turborepo 3.0, and Biome 2.2 - The Low-Overhead Stack**: Summary:
The 2026 “Low-Overhead Stack” centers on consolidating monorepo tooling to reduce configuration and maintenance while boosting performance and AI-readiness. Core components:
- Bun 1.3: Emerges as a unified runtime, package manager, and test runner, replacing npm/pnpm, Jest/Vitest, and often Node.js. Key improvement: Lockfile v3 for monorepo pruning, plus full TypeScript support and native test running.
- Turborepo 3.0 (Canary): Advanced monorepo orchestrator designed for the “Agent Era.” Highlights include turbo docs (local, searchable vector store of code/docs), native Bun workspace support, and improved caching that minimizes CI cache misses.
- Biome 2.2: Consolidates linting/formatting with ecosystem presets (notably thetypescript-monorepo preset), delivering faster performance (Rust-based, ~35x faster than ESLint) and integrated formatting/import organization.

What this means for 2026 monorepos:
- The bottleneck shifts from build speed to complexity management; reducing tool fragmentation is key.
- Duo strategy: Use Bun for runtime/packaging/test needs while maintaining Node.js for legacy or specific environments, enabled by Dual-Runtime Exports in package.json.
- Biome becomes the preferred lint/format tool, with preset-driven configuration to cut setup effort.
- Turborepo coordinates everything with zero-config caching and adds new capabilities like docs indexing and native Bun support to optimize caching and collaboration.
- Lockfile compatibility improvements (Bun Lockfile v3) address prior CI issues, enabling smoother Docker workflows with turbo prune.

If you’re evaluating tooling trends for 2026: prioritize a Bun-based runtime + Turborepo 3.0 for orchestration + Biome 2.2 for lint/format, with careful attention to dual-runtime workflows to preserve Node.js stability where needed.

**How to Pick a Monorepo Tool in 2026 — YoBox**: Summary:

The 2026 landscape for monorepo tooling centers on four main options, each suited to different project profiles:

- pnpm workspaces: Best default for small repos (2–4 packages) with minimal CI overhead. Fast setup, no heavy caching or generators. Simple and low lock-in.
- Turborepo: Strong for TypeScript-heavy monorepos with CI bottlenecks. Emphasizes caching (remote-first) and a low-ceremony workflow, but less opinionated on multi-framework workflows.
- Nx: Ideal for polyglot, enterprise repos that span multiple frameworks/languages. Rich generators, executors, and affected detection. Higher learning curve and potential lock-in, but great consistency across diverse tech stacks.
- Bun workspaces: Best for greenfield, Bun-only projects. Very fast package install and a cohesive, Batteries-included experience, though task running is more limited compared to Turbo/Nx.

Decision guide (quick picks):
1) 2–4 packages, CI under 5 minutes: use pnpm workspaces.
2) Greenfield Bun-first, not needing polyglot support: use Bun workspaces.
3) Many TypeScript packages, CI pain: use Turborepo.
4) Polyglot, multi-framework, willing to adopt opinions: use Nx.

Additional notes:
- Remote caching is a differentiator for Turborepo (works with Vercel out-of-the-box) and is evolving in others.
- Nx’s generators can dramatically reduce boilerplate for multi-app designs (beneficial with design systems and Tailwind v4).
- A single CI entry point and consistent caching strategies (e.g., keyed to lockfile hashes) are more impactful than the chosen tool.
- Bun and Turborepo can coexist (packageManager: bun with Turbo on top).

Bottom line: Pick the simplest tool that addresses your current pain. pnpm for small teams, Turborepo for CI-heavy TS workloads, Nx for polyglot/enterprise needs, or Bun for greenfield Bun-only projects.

  - Small JS team: pnpm workspaces alone.
  - Mid-size JS/TS + Next

**The 2026 Monorepo: Bun 1.3, Turborepo 3.0, and Biome 2.2 - The Low-Overhead Stack**: Summary:
The 2026 “Low-Overhead Stack” centers on consolidating monorepo tooling to reduce configuration and maintenance while boosting performance and AI-readiness. Core components:
- Bun 1.3: Emerges as a unified runtime, package manager, and test runner, replacing npm/pnpm, Jest/Vitest, and often Node.js. Key improvement: Lockfile v3 for monorepo pruning, plus full TypeScript support and native test running.
- Turborepo 3.0 (Canary): Advanced monorepo orchestrator designed for the “Agent Era.” Highlights include turbo docs (local, searchable vector store of code/docs), native Bun workspace support, and improved caching that minimizes CI cache misses.
- Biome 2.2: Consolidates linting/formatting with ecosystem presets (notably thetypescript-monorepo preset), delivering faster performance (Rust-based, ~35x faster than ESLint) and integrated formatting/import organization.

What this means for 2026 monorepos:
- The bottleneck shifts from build speed to complexity management; reducing tool fragmentation is key.
- Duo strategy: Use Bun for runtime/packaging/test needs while maintaining Node.js for legacy or specific environments, enabled by Dual-Runtime Exports in package.json.
- Biome becomes the preferred lint/format tool, with preset-driven configuration to cut setup effort.
- Turborepo coordinates everything with zero-config caching and adds new capabilities like docs indexing and native Bun support to optimize caching and collaboration.
- Lockfile compatibility improvements (Bun Lockfile v3) address prior CI issues, enabling smoother Docker workflows with turbo prune.

If you’re evaluating tooling trends for 2026: prioritize a Bun-based runtime + Turborepo 3.0 for orchestration + Biome 2.2 for lint/format, with careful attention to dual-runtime workflows to preserve Node.js stability where needed.

**How to Pick a Monorepo Tool in 2026 — YoBox**: Summary:

The 2026 landscape for monorepo tooling centers on four main options, each suited to different project profiles:

- pnpm workspaces: Best default for small repos (2–4 packages) with minimal CI overhead. Fast setup, no heavy caching or generators. Simple and low lock-in.
- Turborepo: Strong for TypeScript-heavy monorepos with CI bottlenecks. Emphasizes caching (remote-first) and a low-ceremony workflow, but less opinionated on multi-framework workflows.
- Nx: Ideal for polyglot, enterprise repos that span multiple frameworks/languages. Rich generators, executors, and affected detection. Higher learning curve and potential lock-in, but great consistency across diverse tech stacks.
- Bun workspaces: Best for greenfield, Bun-only projects. Very fast package install and a cohesive, Batteries-included experience, though task running is more limited compared to Turbo/Nx.

Decision guide (quick picks):
1) 2–4 packages, CI under 5 minutes: use pnpm workspaces.
2) Greenfield Bun-first, not needing polyglot support: use Bun workspaces.
3) Many TypeScript packages, CI pain: use Turborepo.
4) Polyglot, multi-framework, willing to adopt opinions: use Nx.

Additional notes:
- Remote caching is a differentiator for Turborepo (works with Vercel out-of-the-box) and is evolving in others.
- Nx’s generators can dramatically reduce boilerplate for multi-app designs (beneficial with design systems and Tailwind v4).
- A single CI entry point and consistent caching strategies (e.g., keyed to lockfile hashes) are more impactful than the chosen tool.
- Bun and Turborepo can coexist (packageManager: bun with Turbo on top).

Bottom line: Pick the simplest tool that addresses your current pain. pnpm for small teams, Turborepo for CI-heavy TS workloads, Nx for polyglot/enterprise needs, or Bun for greenfield Bun-only projects.

content.text:
In **September 2026**, the industry-standard "Low-Overhead Monorepo Stack" (which aligns perfectly with what we are doing in Tau and Sovereign) combines three core technologies:

1. **Bun (v1.4+) as the Runtime & Package Manager:** 
   - Replaces npm/pnpm/yarn with blazing-fast native workspace linking and Lockfile v3.
2. **Turborepo (v2.x/3.x) as the Task Orchestrator:** 
   - Coordinates multi-package builds, tests, and linting with zero-friction caching (`turbo.json`).
3. **Biome (v2.x) as the Linter & Formatter:** 
   - Replaces ESLint/Prettier with a unified Rust-based tool operating ~35x faster.

### How this maps to our structure:
- **Root Workspace:** Declares packages under `packages/*` and `crates/*`.
- **Execution:** `bun run build` resolves dependencies instantly, while Turborepo or our local `buildsrv` daemon handles caching and orchestration.
er what about how we have projects which is a monorepo with many repo or monorepos?

That pattern—where a root directory (`sovereign/`) contains multiple independent repositories or monorepos under `projects/` (like `tau`, `ranch`, `herd`, `shep`)—is known in the industry as a **"Polyrepo-in-a-Monorepo"**, **"Meta-Repo"**, or **"Workspace Mesh"**.

Major tech organizations (and advanced agent/mesh ecosystems like ours) use specific design patterns to handle this cleanly without path confusion:

### 1. The Industry Term: **Meta-Repo / Workspace Mesh**
Instead of forcing everything into a single giant flat monorepo package graph, a **Meta-Repo** acts as an orchestrator holding sovereign sub-projects. Each sub-project (`projects/tau`, `projects/ranch`) is its own self-contained monorepo with its own `package.json`, `Cargo.toml`, or `go.mod`.

### 2. How Teams Manage Meta-Repos in 2026:
- **Workspace-Aware Orchestrators (e.g., Moon or Custom Task Runners):** Tools like `moon` or multi-project build daemons (`buildsrv`) understand directory boundaries. They allow running tasks across specific sub-repos (`buildsrv submit --repo projects/tau ...`) without mixing up dependencies.
- **Strictly Scoped Working Directories:** Each sub-project has its own isolated build cache and lockfile. You *never* run npm/bun commands from the root if the root isn't a package manager workspace; you scope execution directly into `projects/<name>/`.
- **Shared Helpers & Symlinks:** Global utilities, helpers (`helpers/`), and skills (`skills/`) live at the meta-repo root, while service code remains isolated inside `projects/`.

### Why our setup felt confusing earlier:
We tried treating `/home/toxic/estate` like a single flat monorepo package, when it is actually a **Meta-Repo Mesh**. 

- **Meta-Repo Root (`/home/toxic/estate`):** Orchestration, pitching, daemons, shared helpers.
- **Sub-Monorepo (`/home/toxic/estate/projects/tau`):** Dedicated Bun/Cargo workspace for the Tau coding agent.
